 description: Learn how Microsoft Defender for Endpoint provides runtime protection for local AI agents by detecting and blocking prompt injection attacks.
-author: lwainstein
-ms.author: lwainstein
+author: j0shbregman
+ms.author: joshbregman
 ms.service: defender-endpoint
 ms.topic: overview
 ms.custom: msecd-doc-authoring-1030
@@ -102,6 +102,20 @@ Microsoft recommends starting in audit mode to observe detections and validate a
 
 For local PowerShell and organization-wide Microsoft Intune configuration options, see [Set up AI agent runtime protection with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint](configure-ai-agent-runtime-protection).
 
+## Known issues (Preview)
+
+Important
+
+During preview, prompt injection alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal might incorrectly report **Suspicious AI prompt injection blocked** when AI agent runtime protection is configured in **Audit** mode. This is an alert-reporting issue. In Audit mode, runtime protection allows the action to continue and records the detection; the alert title doesn't mean that runtime protection blocked the action.
+
+Verify the runtime protection mode on the affected device as described in [Set up AI agent runtime protection](configure-ai-agent-runtime-protection#enable-runtime-protection). Don't rely on the alert title alone to determine whether an action was blocked. Continue investigating the detection to assess whether the activity is malicious.
+
+Important
+
+During preview, Claude Code might continue processing a tool response even when AI agent runtime protection is configured in **Block** mode and Defender reports a post-tool-response block. This is a blocking limitation, not just an alert-reporting issue. On affected devices, the block alert doesn't mean that runtime protection prevented the agent from processing the detected content.
+
+Don't rely on the alert title alone to determine whether a tool response was blocked. Continue investigating the detection to assess whether the activity is malicious. Post-tool-response inspection occurs after the tool runs and can't undo actions the tool has already completed.
+
 ## Investigation
 
 When runtime protection detects prompt injection, Defender raises a **Suspicious AI prompt injection** alert and correlates related activity into incidents for investigation.

englishSummary.headline: AI agent runtime protection documentation adds preview known issues
englishSummary.summary: The page now documents inaccurate blocked-alert titles in Audit mode and a Claude Code limitation where tool responses may continue after a Block-mode alert.
englishSummary.adminImpact: Check the configured protection mode and investigate detections rather than relying on alert titles. Post-tool-response blocks cannot undo actions already completed.

 ## Review and investigate detections
 
+Important
+
+During preview, a prompt injection alert might incorrectly report a block when runtime protection is configured in Audit mode. In Block mode, Claude Code might continue processing a tool response despite a reported post-tool-response block. See [Known issues (Preview)](ai-agent-runtime-protection-overview#known-issues-preview) for details.
+
 After you enable runtime protection, review alerts to validate detection accuracy and tune your configuration before broadening enforcement. This step is critical during the audit phase because it helps you understand what agents are encountering and whether detections represent real threats.
 
 When runtime protection detects prompt injection, Defender raises a **Suspicious AI prompt injection** alert and takes action based on the configured mode. The alert appears on the device timeline, and related alerts are correlated into incidents for security operations center (SOC) investigation. In block mode, the alert severity is **Critical**, **High**, **Medium**, or **Low** based on assessed risk. In audit mode, the alert is **Informational**, so your team can review what would have been blocked without triaging it as an active threat.

+4. Minimize false positives by overriding spoof for email arriving from the non-Microsoft service. For example, if the non-Microsoft service has an IP address of 172.17.17.35, create two [allowed spoofed sender entries in the Tenant Allow/Block List](tenant-allow-block-list-email-spoof-configure#create-allow-entries-for-spoofed-senders): one External and one Internal as shown in the following screenshot:

     Be sure to remove these override entries if you ever leave the non-Microsoft protection service or change how it functions.
-4. False negative (bad mail allowed) and false positive email submissions to Microsoft should come from the initial version of the message, not the one that returns from the non-Microsoft service. False positives attributed to the non-Microsoft service should be sent to the non-Microsoft service. This requirement can be complex to manage:
+5. False negative (bad mail allowed) and false positive email submissions to Microsoft should come from the initial version of the message, not the one that returns from the non-Microsoft service. False positives attributed to the non-Microsoft service should be sent to the non-Microsoft service. This requirement can be complex to manage:
 
     - **Microsoft false negative (missed at initial reception)**: You need a copy of the message before to delivery to the mailbox. Submit the copy in quarantine from the non-Microsoft service, if it's available.
     - **Microsoft + non-Microsoft service false negative**: If both services miss it, we recommend reporting the original item to Microsoft and reporting the item in the recipient's mailbox to the non-Microsoft service. The item returned to Microsoft 365 from the non-Microsoft service includes details from the non-Microsoft service (for example, the non-Microsoft service's sending IP addresses, custom headers, etc.) which can lead to decreased machine learning effectiveness.

englishSummary.headline: Documentation adds guidance on messages being quarantined again after release
englishSummary.summary: The routing guidance now notes that messages quarantined by the Common Attachments Filter may be quarantined again after release because of the return mail-flow path. It also clarifies that submissions to Microsoft should use the initial message version.
englishSummary.adminImpact: Administrators using this routing topology should account for possible repeat quarantine and follow the updated submission guidance; no required action is stated.
